text: Adam Smith's diamond-water paradox: water is essential yet nearly free, diamonds inessential yet costly. Marginal utility resolved it: price tracks the value of one more unit, not of the whole supply.
Giffen goods, whose demand rises with their price, were long thought nearly mythical. In 2008 Robert Jensen and Nolan Miller found poor households in Hunan, China, buying more rice as it got pricier.
The paradox of thrift: if everyone tries to save more during a slump, spending falls, incomes shrink, and total savings can end up no higher, or even lower, than before.
"But this long run is a misleading guide to current affairs. In the long run we are all dead." (John Maynard Keynes, A Tract on Monetary Reform, 1923)
"The welfare of a nation can, therefore, scarcely be inferred from a measurement of national income as defined above." (Simon Kuznets, National Income, 1929–1932, 1934)

Instrumental variables, a core tool of econometrics, first appeared in 1928 in an appendix to Philip Wright's book on tariffs on animal and vegetable oils. A 2003 stylometric study credited him, not his son Sewall.

In Robert Axelrod's 1980 computer tournaments of the repeated prisoner's dilemma, the winner was the simplest entry: Anatol Rapoport's tit for tat, which cooperates first and then copies its opponent's last move.
In a 1974 study by Tversky and Kahneman, people saw a wheel of fortune land on 10 or 65 before estimating the share of African countries in the UN. Their median guesses: 25% and 45%.

The 'hot hand' in basketball was called a fallacy in 1985. In 2018 Joshua Miller and Adam Sanjurjo showed the original analysis had a subtle statistical bias; corrected, the data suggest a modest hot hand.

Isaac Newton supposedly lost about £20,000 in the South Sea Bubble of 1720, though the evidence is thin. His remark that he 'could not calculate the madness of the people' is secondhand, first printed in 1820.
The Dutch East India Company, founded in 1602, is often called the first publicly traded company: its shares changed hands in Amsterdam, a model for the stock markets that followed.
On Yap in Micronesia, huge limestone discs called rai served as money, and ownership changed without the stones moving. One, lost at sea in transit, reportedly still counted as its family's wealth.
Song dynasty China began issuing government paper money, jiaozi, in Sichuan in 1024, after private merchant notes there failed. Sichuan's heavy iron coins had made paper especially welcome.
Hungary's 1946 hyperinflation is the worst on record: at its peak, prices doubled about every 15 hours, and the government issued a banknote worth 100 quintillion pengő.
Most money is created not by central banks but by commercial banks making loans: each new loan creates a matching deposit, as the Bank of England explained in a 2014 bulletin.
Mathematician Stanislaw Ulam challenged Paul Samuelson to name one idea in the social sciences that is both true and non-trivial. Samuelson's answer, years later: Ricardo's comparative advantage.
In 1992 New Jersey raised its minimum wage; David Card and Alan Krueger compared fast-food jobs there with neighboring Pennsylvania and found no drop in employment. Card won a 2021 Nobel.
In 2023 Claudia Goldin became the first woman to win the economics Nobel unshared, for her work tracing women's earnings and work across more than 200 years of US history.
Thomas Malthus warned in 1798 that population would outrun food. The world then had under 1 billion people; it passed 8 billion in 2022, while food supply per person rose.
In 1902 French-ruled Hanoi paid a bounty per rat tail to fight plague. Residents cut off tails and released the rats to breed, and inspectors found rat farms: a classic case of perverse incentives.

Elinor Ostrom, the first woman to win the economics Nobel (2009), showed through field studies that communities often manage shared forests, pastures and fisheries well, against the 'tragedy of the commons'.

In 1924 the world's main light bulb makers, including Osram, Philips and GE, formed the Phoebus cartel, then fined members whose bulbs lasted over 1,000 hours, down from the 1,500 to 2,000 hours once common.
Thomas Carlyle coined 'the dismal science' in an 1849 essay defending slavery. His target was less Malthus's gloomy forecasts than the economists who supported emancipation and free labor.
Monopoly descends from The Landlord's Game, patented by Lizzie Magie in 1904 to show how land rents enrich owners and impoverish tenants, as a case for Henry George's land tax.
William Vickrey showed that in a sealed second-price auction, bidding your true value is the best strategy. He won the economics Nobel on 8 October 1996 and died three days later.
Mancur Olson's 1965 Logic of Collective Action explains why small, concentrated interests often beat large, diffuse ones: each member of a small group gains enough to bother organizing.
On 22 May 2010 Laszlo Hanyecz paid 10,000 bitcoins for two Papa John's pizzas, the first well-known purchase of physical goods with bitcoin. Fans mark the date as Bitcoin Pizza Day.
Bitcoin's first block, mined in January 2009, embeds a newspaper headline: 'The Times 03/Jan/2009 Chancellor on brink of second bailout for banks'.
Adam Smith's 'invisible hand' appears only once in The Wealth of Nations (1776), in a passage on merchants preferring to invest at home, and just once in The Theory of Moral Sentiments.
Muhammad Yunus began microcredit in 1976 by lending a total of $27 to 42 women in the Bangladeshi village of Jobra. Later randomized trials found its average effects on income modest.
